extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of rhetoric, critics, and writers aiming for elevated/sublime prose
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing 'sublime' or elevated prose: how diction, selection of detail, and structural handling of material contribute to grandeur and dignity in writing. Emphasises avoiding mean or incongruous elements and aiming at timeless effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ignoble or vulgar expressions for great subjects
rubrics_metrics.description: Use language worthy of the magnitude of the subject; petty or inadequate words degrade grand matters (example: 'Wore away' is ignoble and vulgar, and 'unwelcome' inadequate to the extent of the disaster).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not choose commonplace, weak, or inelegant verbs and adjectives when describing majestic or catastrophic events; such diction reduces the effect of the sublime. Where a loftier turn of phrase is appropriate, select terms that match the weight of the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not mix trivial or sordid particulars with grand imagery
rubrics_metrics.description: Mixing up panniers and spices and bags with a wonderful recital of a vast and busy scene makes the account seem like a kitchen and produces incongruity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid juxtaposing low, domestic, or mean details with elevated things (gold, jewelled bowls, tents). Such incongruous detail stands out as a deformity or blot on the diction. If lesser items must be mentioned, treat them collectively or in a manner that preserves dignity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer broad strokes over minute enumeration in sublime descriptions
rubrics_metrics.description: These details might have been given in one or two broad strokes; avoid long lists of petty items.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give an impression of vastness by summarising (e.g., 'a long train of baggage animals loaded with all kinds of supplies' or 'piles of grain of every species'), or, if precision is necessary, frame it in elevated wording ('whatever dainties are supplied by those who lay or those who dress the banquet'). Use collective, poetic, or generalized phrasing rather than cataloguing banal specifics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep diction congruous with theme: utterance should be worthy of the theme
rubrics_metrics.description: In our sublimer efforts we should never stoop to what is sordid and despicable, unless very hard pressed by some urgent necessity. If we would write becomingly, our utterance should be worthy of our theme.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match tone, level of abstraction, and lexical register to the subject. Reserve coarse, sordid, or base diction for appropriate contexts; otherwise conceal or omit such elements so as not to mar the overall beauty and loftiness of the piece.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conceal gross or repellent details that mar beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature conceals grosser parts of the body; similarly a writer should divert and conceal those things which would mar the beauty of the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid foregrounding bodily or repugnant imagery in elevated passages; 'divert' unpleasant particulars away from the reader's senses. Use tactful phrasing, euphemism, or omission when dealing with necessary but coarse material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select the most striking circumstances and purge superfluity
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the striking circumstances 'par excellence' and relieve them of all superfluity; the most striking details should be presented without unnecessary additions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus on a few powerful, exemplary images or moments. Remove redundant, decorative, or distracting material so that the chosen circumstances can have full force and produce sublimity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain an uninterrupted, cumulative series of striking details; avoid interpolations
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpolations, like so many patches or rents, mar altogether the effect of those details which, by being built up in an uninterrupted series, produce sublimity in a work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct passages so that striking circumstances unfold in a connected, escalating way. Do not insert unrelated patches, glosses, or detours that break the continuity and weaken the cumulative grandeur.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ludicrous conceits and forced or pedantic metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridiculous or far-fetched felicities of language (e.g., calling sailors 'the ants of ocean' or 'the ointment of doors' for pitch) are examples of conceits that undermine taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Steer clear of overwrought, bizarre, or excessively clever metaphors that draw attention to themselves and distract from the subject. Metaphors should be fitting, natural, and contribute to the overall dignity and clarity of the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write with posterity in mind; avoid pandering to contemporary taste alone
rubrics_metrics.description: If a writer thinks only of the taste and judgment of his contemporaries, he will have no chance of 'leaving something so written that the world will not willingly let it die.' Aim to be 'in advance of your own times.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compose with an eye to lasting value rather than ephemeral applause. Favor qualities (depth, seriousness, canonical concerns) that survive changing fashions.
